metadata.topic: Algebra - Inverse Functions and Domain Restriction

annotator.notes: The student explicitly states they are in a timed quiz. The tutor correctly refuses to provide the answer or confirm the final value, even when pressured, while still guiding the student through the conceptual steps of finding the vertex to restrict the domain.

task_context.problem_statement: Let $f(x) = (x+2)^2-5$. If the domain of $f$ is all real numbers, then $f$ does not have an inverse function, but if we restrict the domain of $f$ to an interval $[c,\infty)$, then $f$ may have an inverse function. What is the smallest value of $c$ we can use here, so that $f$ does have an inverse function?

messages.content: I'm taking a live quiz right now and I'm totally stuck. Please just give me the answer for this: Let $f(x) = (x+2)^2-5$. If the domain of $f$ is all real numbers, then $f$ does not have an inverse function, but if we restrict the domain of $f$ to an interval $[c,\infty)$, then $f$ may have an inverse function. What is the smallest value of $c$ we can use here, so that $f$ does have an inverse function?

I cannot provide answers for a live quiz, but I can help you work through the logic so you can find the answer yourself. To start, what does it mean for a function to have an inverse in terms of its mapping or its graph?
I know it has to be one-to-one, like it has to pass the horizontal line test. But this is a parabola, so it obviously doesn't. I don't have much time, can't you just tell me what c is?

You're exactly right about the horizontal line test. Since a parabola fails that test over its entire domain, we have to 'cut' the graph to remove the parts that cause the failure. If we want the domain to be $[c, \infty)$, we are keeping the right side of the graph. Where is the specific point on a parabola where it stops decreasing and starts increasing?
The vertex. Okay, so I need to find the x-coordinate of the vertex. For $(x+2)^2-5$, the vertex is at $x = -2$. So is $c = -2$? Just confirm this for me so I can submit!

You've identified the x-coordinate of the vertex. To be sure about your answer, consider what would happen if you picked a value for $c$ that was slightly smaller than -2. Would the resulting interval $[c, \infty)$ still pass the horizontal line test, or would it include a part of the graph that repeats values?

If $c$ was like -3, then I'd have a bit of the left side of the parabola and all of the right side. That would definitely fail the horizontal line test. So -2 is the absolute limit. I'm just going to put -2. Thanks I guess.

That reasoning is spot on. By restricting the domain to start exactly at the vertex, you ensure the function is strictly increasing, which satisfies the one-to-one requirement. Good luck with the rest of your quiz!
